Operation manual   /   Getting started

Gear based synthesizer

Imagine a gear with 120 little teeth rotating once every second. Every time makes a full turn, you hear a click. Stick another gear into the machine with half as many teeth and it clicks twice before the first gear comes round again.

A gear with 1/3rd as many teeth (40 teeth) spins around and clicks three times in the same time giving you the familiar "Nice-cuppa tea" hemiola. If you speed up the train those clicks meld together after about 20hz in your brainhole to become pitches of a brand saw-tooth oscillator palying an OCTAVE and a FIFTH. The two-click (2:1 ratio) gear sounds an octave above the root (1:1 Ratio). The three-click gear (3:1) sounds an octave and a fifth above it. The harmony was already there in the rhythm... YIKES!

Count one turn of the root

Gear teethTurns per root turnRoot at 2 HzRoot at 110 Hz
12012 clicks/s110 Hz · A
6024 clicks/s220 Hz · A
4036 clicks/s330 Hz · E, a pure fifth above 220 Hz

Gear frequency = root frequency × root teeth ÷ gear teeth. Teeth set the speed ratio. Each revolution supplies one waveform cycle. In the editor a minus sign on a ratio records the opposite rotation of meshed neighbours. Use the magnitude to read the musical interval.

Hear the same ratio at two speeds

In the slow example, listen for the root accent and count the subdivisions. In the fast example, listen for the three pitches together. These short illustrations play in this guide.

Turn a three-gear train

Drag the crank handle to turn the root by hand. Or leave Follow frequency on and move the slider from 0 to 440 Hz. The other gears follow their ratios. Sound is optional.

Moving at 1.0 Hz. Gear 2 makes 2 turns; Gear 3 makes 3 turns per root turn.
The crank drives the 120-tooth root. Each mesh reverses direction; the 2:1 and 3:1 settings make two and three turns for every root turn. At high rates the picture reaches its smooth display limit; the audio continues to follow the slider up to 440 Hz.

Where to go next

For your first session, follow Quick start. To hear a one-tooth change as a natural chorus, open Build a near-unison pair. To turn one gear into a pitch control for another, go to Connect two gears for FM.

Operation manual   /   Getting started

Install and open TuneOut

TuneOut 0.3.6 is a Windows x64 and Linux x86_64 VST3 instrument. The DAW supplies the audio engine, MIDI input and output routing for the instrument’s sound.

  1. Close the DAW and extract the entire ZIP. On Windows, run Windows/Install TuneOut.cmd. On Linux, copy the whole Linux/TuneOut.vst3 folder into ~/.vst3/. Start Here.txt lists the system requirements.
  2. Open Nuendo or Cubase. Add an instrument track and choose TuneOut. In Ableton Live, place TuneOut from the VST3 instruments list on a MIDI track.
  3. Open the plug-in editor and click a coloured key at the bottom. On Linux, add TuneOut in your native VST3 instrument host. For a physical keyboard, choose its MIDI port as the track input and enable monitoring or record-arm. Route the track to your stereo output.
Result A new instance opens on Chordial with a detached Moiré window. Hold a key for several seconds to hear the patch open. Reopening a saved project recalls its own sound.

Missing from the instrument list? See Troubleshooting.

‹ One click per revolutionQuick start · turn rhythm into harmony ›
Operation manual   /   Getting started

Quick start · turn rhythm into harmony

You will make a three-gear train that plays the first three harmonics from one key. Allow about five minutes. Begin with an open TuneOut instrument track.

  1. At the top of the editor select Happy New Gear. This gives you one 120-tooth root. Set Bloom to 0 and play one note.
  2. Select the root card. Under Oscillator choose Waveform → Sawtooth and set Shape / noise width to 0.50. The ramp resets once per turn.
  3. Click + 2:1 under the gear cards. The new 60-tooth gear makes two turns for each root turn. Hold the same key, mute and unmute this gear, and listen for the octave.
  4. Click + 3:1. This adds a 40-tooth gear. Mute the root for a moment and listen to the pure fifth between the 60- and 40-tooth gears. Unmute the root to hear the whole train.
  5. To slow the train down, set Fundamental (Hz) to 2 and hold MIDI note 69 (A). Listen for the saw resets. Restore 110 Hz on that same key to hear 110, 220 and 330 Hz. If your speakers roll off the very low gears, use the click illustration on the opening page.
  6. Choose Save preset and name the patch “Three harmonics”.
Result Playing a different note moves the whole harmony. The tooth counts keep the three pitches in the same proportions. You have made this sound using only mechanical connections.
‹ Install and open TuneOutBuild a near-unison pair · 120:119 ›
Operation manual   /   Getting started

Build a near-unison pair · 120:119

Two 120-tooth gears turn at exactly the same rate. Change one to 119 teeth. It gains one whole revolution every 119 root revolutions. You hear that slow drift as beats in a sustained note.

  1. Load Happy New Gear. Use + GEAR → Harmonics → 1:1. Select the new gear and set both gears to Sine / shaped with Shape at 0.50. Give them similar volumes.
  2. Set Fundamental to 220 Hz and hold MIDI note 69. With both gears at 120 teeth the amplitudes keep a fixed relationship.
  3. Select the added gear. In Oscillator → Teeth, enter 119. Keep the root at 120. Listen to the note swell and dip.
  4. Try 440 Hz with the same key. Doubling the root frequency doubles the beat rate. Restore 120 teeth on the added gear to return to unison.
Root119-tooth gearDifference / beat rate
110 Hz110.92 Hz0.92 beats/s
220 Hz221.85 Hz1.85 beats/s
440 Hz443.70 Hz3.70 beats/s

The 120:119 ratio is about 14.49 cents wide. This is a natural chorus-like beating between two sources. You can hear it in mono. Try sawtooth on both gears next: different pairs of harmonics beat at different rates, giving the sound more movement.

Editor overview

Top two rows
Choose a sound, set the pitch reference, balance Master and Bloom, or open the detached display.
Left column
Each card is one sound source. Scroll here to reach more gears. A cyan cable means one gear is feeding another’s FM input.
Middle column
The selector identifies the gear you are editing. Gold is its volume envelope, green is modulation, and cyan is auxiliary. Each graph has its own Expand control.
Right column
The eight inspector tabs organise settings for the selected gear and the instrument. Scroll inside a tab to see additional controls.
Bottom strip
Play notes, change keyboard tuning, toggle performance modes, or set your bend range. Read the status line after a routing or file operation.
‹ Build a near-unison pair · 120:119Performance settings · Keyboard shortcuts and mouse commands ›

Performance settings and live controls

Start a new patch

Click New Patch beside the preset controls for a single 120-tooth sawtooth root at 440 Hz. Add gears to build your instrument. Save a patch you want to keep before starting a new one.

Turn the machine by hand

Choose Steampunk or Neon and enable Hand crank. Drag the grip around the separate chain wheel to the left of the machine. With New Patch, two turns per second produce two audible knocks per second. Add a 60-tooth gear to the 120-tooth root and its oscillator runs twice as fast. Each gear follows its volume, envelope and routing in the instrument. Release the handle to stop the crank. The DAW must be processing the instrument; you can leave the keyboard alone.

Read the rotation speed

During keyboard playback, a bright mark follows each wheel at its real rotation rate up to 30 Hz. Beyond that point, indicated rotation increases on a compressed scale. Wider spoke trails, brighter curved highlights and slight jitter help distinguish fast gears. Display refresh and host load affect how much motion you can see.

See the tooth sweep

A sweeping gear changes its pitch radius and moves its descendants as it grows or shrinks. For a clear demonstration, sweep a child between 60 and 120 teeth. The selected metal finish stays stable as it turns. Gears warm above 1 kHz, glow blue from 10 kHz and reach white at 20 kHz.

Set divisions and period

For 12 EDO, drag Divisions to 12 and Period ratio to 2:1. For the Bohlen–Pierce division of the tritave, choose 13 and 3:1. Normal drags snap to integers. Hold Ctrl while dragging either control for fractional values. The period field also accepts ratios such as 3:2.

Move envelopes together

Drag an attack or release handle on the gear graph to scale that time across the gears. For instance, if two gears start at 10 ms and 30 ms, doubling the first to 20 ms gives 60 ms on the second. Decay and sustain work the same way. Edits stay within the chosen envelope family (Volume, Modulation or Auxiliary) and each control’s range. Starting a drag from zero uses an additive change. Ctrl-drag affects only the selected gear. The same rule applies in the expanded graph and on the inspector’s A/D/S/R sliders.

Recall your reference pitch

Click the number between Fundamental and its slider to return to 440 Hz. To use another reference, set Fundamental to your preferred frequency and right-click the number. For example, store 432 Hz before trying a different pitch. The next click recalls 432 Hz.

Play a familiar chord in an equal division

Choose equal divisions in Tuning files, open the Tuning inspector, set Divisions to 24 and leave Period at 2. Enable Scale Quantize and select C and Chromatic. Play C–E–G on your usual keys. Each key now selects a nearby step of the 24-note tuning. A positive wheel movement beyond the centre band raises the entire chord by one 50-cent step. Returning the wheel to centre brings it back.

Choose the wheel and scale behaviour

15 EDO gives one step each way. 24 EDO also gives one. In 31 EDO the wheel moves through −2, −1, 0, +1 and +2. The centre band is 60–68 on the web instrument’s 0–128 control scale. In 12 EDO, with Scale Quantize off, or with a file-based tuning, the ordinary Bend Range applies. Major and Minor aim the scale notes at just intervals before rounding to the grid. Other keys stay playable. In an octave tuning, a held major, minor, diminished, augmented or suspended triad uses a common chord root.

Change teeth while playing

Hover over the tooth count at the top of a gear card and scroll up or down. One notch changes the gear by one tooth. For a near-unison chorus, start with a 120-tooth root and a 120-tooth child. Hold a note and scroll the child down to 119.

Sweep between two tooth counts

Right-click the tooth count and choose Set tooth range and travel time. For a slowly drifting chorus enter 119 and 120 with a travel time of four seconds. Click Apply range. The sweep goes to the far endpoint in four seconds and returns in another four. Untick Quantize to whole teeth for continuous travel, or tick it to hear distinct gear ratios. Choose Stop tooth sweep to return to the manually set count. The root sets the reference pitch. Sweeping its teeth changes the ratios of connected gears.

Reset and route controls

Ctrl-click a gear knob or inspector slider to set it to zero. Where zero is outside the control’s range, the control stops at its nearest allowed value. Right-click the Volume, FM Index, Pan or Shape slider to open the corresponding gear knob menu. Choose MIDI Learn to assign a controller, Min / Max for timed motion, or Send to Aux ADSR for note-triggered movement.

Set up your keyboard and workspace

Open the gear icon at the upper left. Coloured keys controls the keyboard palette. Light played notes controls note feedback independently. Invert key colours changes the key appearance. Subharmonics only on lowest held note applies to the current patch. Show ADSR playback dot displays the active stage of the selected gear during playback.

Choose defaults for future sessions

Set your divisions, then use Use current divisions for new instances. Store the current patch for startup or choose Restore Chordial startup. Select a startup visualizer, including Off. You can also save the current Moiré background, choose the fresh gear waveform, or copy the previous gear’s tone and envelopes. Audio output devices and incoming MIDI ports are selected in the DAW.

‹ Editor overviewGear train and mechanical connections ›
Operation manual   /   Control reference

Gear train and mechanical connections

Think of the root gear as the pitch you play. Each connected gear can add another pitch, bend another gear through FM, or do both.

ROOT / GEAR · teeth · ratio
The number after ROOT or GEAR identifies the part. With a 120-tooth root, a 60-tooth neighbour turns twice as fast and sounds an octave above. The minus sign on a ratio shows reverse rotation. A smaller gear can have a higher pitch even when it turns backwards.
+ 1:2 · + 2:1 · + 3:1 · + 4:1
Add a sub-octave, octave, octave-plus-fifth or two octaves, respectively. New gears connect to the root. A dimmed shortcut means the ratio cannot be made with a supported whole tooth count.
+ GEAR
Open Harmonics or Subharmonics for more ratios. The palette offers reduced fractions with numerator and denominator up to 32 that fit the current root teeth. A 120-tooth root admits 5:1 exactly. A root divisible by 7 admits 7:1.
REMOVE · SET ROOT
Remove the selected gear or make it the new pitch reference. Changing the root can retune the entire train. Save a copy before reorganising a favourite sound.
Volume · Mute · Solo
Drag Volume vertically to set how much of this gear reaches the mix. Mute silences its audible contribution. Solo lets you listen to selected parts together. An FM source can continue bending its receiver even with its own Volume at zero.
FM · Pan · Shape
FM sets the incoming modulation amount, from 0 to 8. Pan sets the angle used for spatial placement. Shape changes tooth or noise width from 0 to 0.98. Double-click Shape to cycle oscillator waveforms. Right-click any of the four knobs for assignment options.
FM IN · FM OUT · CANCEL
FM OUT arms the source. Click the receiving card to finish the cable, or drag from the source’s FM OUT and release on the receiver. Click CANCEL to disarm. Click an occupied IN label to unplug.
A mechanical connection sets pitch and rotation. An FM cable carries a changing signal into another oscillator’s pitch. Adding a gear makes the mechanical connection automatically. You decide whether to add the FM cable.
‹ Keyboard shortcuts and mouse commandsConnect two gears for FM ›
Operation manual   /   Frequency modulation

Connect two gears for FM

For a first FM sound, give one gear the job of making a clean tone and a second gear the job of bending it. The receiving gear is the carrier. The sending gear is the modulator.

  1. Load Happy New Gear. Select the root and choose Oscillator → Waveform → Sine / shaped. Set Shape to 0.50.
  2. Click + 2:1. On the new gear choose Sine / shaped, set Shape to 0.50 and lower its Volume to zero. Now you can hear the carrier on its own.
  3. Click FM OUT on the new gear, then click the root card. Hold a key. Drag the root’s FM knob from zero towards 1. The extra harmonics you hear come from the modulation.
  4. Double-click the root’s FM knob and choose Direct, then try cube or tanh on the same note. Compare them at the same FM amount. To hear the starting tone again, turn the amount down to zero.
FM enabled
Switch the receiver’s FM processing on or off for comparison.
FM source gear
Choose the sender by its gear ID. Each receiver has one input. One source can feed several receivers. You can also make a chain, such as gear 3 into gear 2 into the root. Feedback loops are blocked.
FM index
Controls the size of the pitch deviation. Start below 1 for a gentle change. Raise it for more pronounced sidebands. The result depends on both pitches, the source waveform and the function.
FM function
Shapes the modulation signal before it bends the receiver. Direct passes the source through. Open the FM equation reference to look up its frequency response.
FM scope
Choose Wave / Moiré, open its controls and enable FM scope. Watch the summed audio while holding one note and sweeping the receiver’s FM knob. A chord or a beating patch can produce a moving trace even with triggering.
‹ Gear train and mechanical connectionsRead an FM equation ›
Operation manual   /   Frequency modulation

Read an FM equation

The receiver already has a pitch from the gear train. FM changes how quickly its oscillator moves through its next cycle. The equation decides how far the current sample of the sending gear pushes that rate up or down.

Signal path

  1. Read the sender. Its current waveform value lies between −1 and +1. Call this value x. Zero is the middle of the waveform.
  2. Apply the equation. Direct uses x itself. Other choices reshape it into a signed bend value. The FM index can also change the shape of the function.
  3. Convert the bend to hertz. Multiply the signed bend by the sender’s frequency magnitude and the receiver’s effective FM index. Add the result to the carrier’s current base frequency.
Instantaneous carrier rate (Hz)
Carrier base Hz + shaped sender value × sender Hz × FM index

At index zero there is no frequency shift. For transformed functions the internal shape parameter is limited to 0.1–8. Below index 1, TuneOut blends the reshaped value with Direct, then limits the result to ±1. The outer index still sets deviation depth. At extreme settings the engine limits the signed rate to ±45% of the sample rate. A negative rate means the oscillator phase runs backwards.

One setup for all the examples

Use a 440 Hz root carrier and a 220 Hz sine sender. In Happy New Gear, add + 1:2, set the new gear to Sine / shaped with width 0.50, turn its Volume down and patch its FM OUT to the root. Choose a circular gear, zero Off-centre and FM index 1 on the receiver. A steady A at MIDI 69 gives the reference pitches. The numbers below are instantaneous oscillator rates. A tuner listening to the whole note can report something different.

Einstein mass energy · E=mc²

TuneOut uses the square-law idea as a musical transfer curve. The sender’s magnitude is squared and its sign is restored: y = sign(x) × |x|². Index 1 and a +0.5 sample give +0.25 × 220 Hz, so the carrier reaches 495 Hz. Direct reaches 550 Hz at that same instant. A −0.5 sample gives 385 Hz. At the ±1 peaks both equations reach 220 and 660 Hz. The difference is how long the pitch stays near 440 Hz between peaks. The label refers to this curve; the calculation uses waveform amplitude, with no mass or speed-of-light input.

Mandelbrot · what happens inside the set?

For each source sample TuneOut starts z at zero and chooses a point c = (0.85x − 0.15) + i(0.08 × shape parameter). It repeats z ← z² + c up to six times, testing whether |z| has exceeded 2 before each update. If the count is n, the bend is sign(x) × (n/3 − 1) before blending and limiting.

A point that stays within the boundary for all six checks produces a full signed bend. At index 1, +0.5 lasts six iterations, so the carrier runs at 660 Hz. At +0.75 it lasts five, giving 586.67 Hz. At +1 the count is three and the carrier returns to 440 Hz. A six-step test groups many nearby samples on the same shelf. As the sine wave moves between shelves, the carrier jumps between rates. The calculation starts afresh on every sample. Six iterations classify the point for this sound; they cannot establish mathematical membership for every boundary point.

Sender sampleDirectEinstein mass energyMandelbrot
−0.50330 Hz385 Hz220 Hz
0440 Hz440 Hz440 Hz
+0.50550 Hz495 Hz660 Hz
+0.75605 Hz563.75 Hz586.67 Hz
+1.00660 Hz660 Hz440 Hz

Open the equation explorer to change the index or inspect a particular input value. The following reference topics describe every entry in the receiver’s equation menu.

Operation manual   /   Frequency modulation

Equation explorer

Choose any equation. The horizontal axis is its input, from −1 to +1. The vertical axis is the resulting frequency around a 440 Hz carrier. The input slider lets you sweep that value and hear the equation on one oscillator. There is no sender oscillator or second FM stage in this example.

Move this slider to send changing input values through the selected equation. The equation moves one oscillator around a 440 Hz carrier.

Audio stopped.

The horizontal dashed line marks the unmodulated 440 Hz carrier. Each trace uses the same 220 Hz deviation scale; the index sets how far the equation moves that one oscillator. Read the vertical labels when comparing indices because the plotted range expands with the possible deviation.

‹ Read an FM equationRoute a knob to Aux ADSR ›
Operation manual   /   Working procedures

Route a knob to Aux ADSR

Try making a note start glassy and settle into a softer tone. Keep the FM cable from the previous example. This time the key press will turn the receiver’s FM knob for you.

  1. On the receiving gear, right-click FM → Min / Max range…. Set Minimum to 0.8 and Maximum to 3.2. Click Apply range. At this point the knob travels back and forth on a timer.
  2. Right-click the same knob and choose Send to Aux ADSR. The knob shows AUX. The cyan graph now names the assigned knob. This selects the note envelope as the driver.
  3. Open Envelopes. Set Aux ADSR Depth to 1.00. Try Aux Attack 0.010 s, Decay 0.250 s, Sustain 0.25, and Release 0.180 s. Leave enough Volume Release to hear the end.
  4. Play a note. FM rises from 0.8 to 3.2, then settles at about 1.4 while you hold it. Release brings FM back towards 0.8. Lengthen Aux Attack for a tone that brightens gradually.
Minimum / Maximum
These are real knob values. Volume uses 0–100%, FM uses 0–8, Pan uses −180° to +180°, and Shape uses 0–0.98. A higher Minimum than Maximum reverses the sweep.
Travel time · Apply range
Set 0.01–60 s for one journey between the endpoints. A 1 s journey takes 2 s to go there and back. The timed sweep runs on the audio clock and is shared across notes. Applying a range to an existing Aux assignment keeps the envelope in control.
Send to Aux ADSR
One of the four card knobs per gear can follow this envelope. Assigning another knob on that gear moves the route. Other gears each have their own Aux envelope. The command enables Aux and clears the inspector’s separate Aux target.
Aux ADSR target · Depth
Use the inspector target for Shape width, FM index, Pan or Off-centre. For a right-click knob assignment, leave this target at None. Depth scales the envelope’s influence. At zero, an assigned knob stays at Minimum. At 1 it can reach Maximum.
Remove modulation
Returns the knob to manual or learned-CC operation. Clear MIDI assignment separately if you also want to detach the hardware controller.
MIDI Learn · Clear MIDI assignment · Cancel MIDI Learn
Learn waits for a control-change message on the instrument track. Clear forgets the linked CC. Cancel stops listening for the next assignment. The right-click menu shows the learned CC number and MIDI channel.
For a hand-played variation, choose Min / Max range, set the endpoints, then choose MIDI Learn and move a hardware knob. Learning selects CC control and retains those endpoints. A timed or enabled Aux route takes priority until you remove its modulation.
‹ Equation explorerVolume, Modulation and Auxiliary ADSR ›
Operation manual   /   Control reference

Volume, Modulation and Auxiliary ADSR

An envelope is a little performance that begins with each note. A pluck, a bowed attack, a repeating shimmer and a fading tail can all begin with the same oscillator.

Volume ADSR
Sets the loudness of this gear per note. Short attack and decay with low sustain make a pluck. A longer attack and high sustain suit a pad.
Modulation ADSR
Click the green graph title or use Mod ADSR Enabled. In Envelopes choose Mod ADSR Target. Shape width can change tone colour, FM index can tame a bright attack, Pan can move the sound towards its placed position, and Off-centre can bring wobble in over time.
Auxiliary ADSR
An independent second modulation envelope. Click its title or use Auxiliary ADSR Enabled. A separate Aux envelope lets the tone brighten while the Volume envelope is already fading.
Attack · peak level
The first large handle sets rise time horizontally and peak level vertically. Attack is measured in seconds in the inspector. Enter 0.009 for 9 ms.
Decay · Sustain
Decay sets how long the peak takes to reach the sustain level. Sustain is a level from 0 to 1, displayed as a percentage on the graph. Hold a key to hear it.
Release
Time from key-up, or sustain-pedal lift, to the end. Release begins from the current level, even when you release midway through attack or a sustain loop. Attack, decay and release each span 0–10 s.
Attack / Decay / Release curve
Drag the small middle handle to bend a stage, or enter a curve from −1 to +1 in Envelopes. Zero is linear for a plain stage. A point drawn into a stage gives that stage its own path.
Expand · custom points
Open the detailed graph. Double-click inside a stage to add a point, drag it to set time and level, and right-click it to remove it. Click outside the panel to return.
Sustain window · Loop sustain
Set the sustain path’s duration from 0.05 to 30 s. Add points between decay and release to make audible movement. Loop sustain repeats that path while held. With looping off it runs once and settles. A flat path sounds steady either way.
For your 9 ms attack and 0 ms decay, the first sustain cycle begins 9 ms after note-on, rounded to the nearest sample. Bloom can still fade that gear into the mix while its loop is running.
‹ Route a knob to Aux ADSROscillator and tooth shape ›
Operation manual   /   Control reference

Oscillator and tooth shape

Open Oscillator for the selected gear. Three controls with similar names do different jobs here.

Source
Oscillator makes a pitched wave. Filtered noise is useful for air, breath or percussion. Audio sample reads the recording loaded in the Sample tab.
Waveform
Sine / shaped gives a simple FM starting point at width 0.50. Triangle is gentler than a saw. Sawtooth is useful for a bright sustained layer. Square gives a hollow tone and responds strongly to width. Clockwork adds a short strike. Double-clicking the card’s Shape knob cycles through these five choices.
Shape / noise width
Changes the oscillator pulse or contour, depending on waveform. On Square it changes pulse width. On Sawtooth, raising it above 0.50 blends towards a smoother wave. On filtered noise it changes the band of frequencies that passes. Try moving it slowly during one held note.
Gear shape
Sets the mechanical motion profile. Choose circular, ellipse, square, hexagon, triangle, rectangle, cardioid, heart or mobius. Start circular when comparing precise gear ratios. Other profiles can vary the rate as the mechanism turns.
Teeth
1–15,015 whole teeth. A smaller driven gear rotates faster. Editing a parent or the root can change the pitch relationship of other connected gears. The card updates its ratio.
Gear volume · Mute gear · Solo gear
These mirror the card controls. Volume here uses 0–1, so 0.25 is 25%. When summing several loud gears, lower Master or individual volumes to leave headroom.
‹ Volume, Modulation and Auxiliary ADSRKeyboard, tuning files and glissando ›
Operation manual   /   Control reference

Keyboard, tuning files and glissando

The coloured keyboard is a quick way to hear the patch. A controller or a recorded MIDI clip plays the same native instrument through your DAW.

Coloured keys · Oct − / Oct +
Click or touch to audition, drag across keys to change notes, and release to stop. Octave buttons shift the visible five-octave keyboard. Incoming MIDI keeps its own note numbers.
Fundamental (Hz)
Sets the pitch reference from 0.5 to 2,000 Hz. With ordinary 12-tone tuning, MIDI note 69 follows this frequency. Happy New Gear starts at 440 Hz. Very low values are useful for rhythmic experiments.
JI chord tuning
While you hold a chord, the instrument seeks nearby simple frequency ratios relative to a chord root. Try a sustained major third with JI on and off and listen for changes in beating. Turn JI off when you want the exact steps in an imported scale.
Polyphonic · Gliss
Polyphonic lets notes overlap, with up to ten held voices and ten release tails. Turn it off for a mono lead. Enable Gliss and overlap two notes to hear the new pitch glide from the previous held note.
Hold mono notes
In the Tuning tab, enable this to keep the mono note sounding after key-up. Play the next note to change pitch. Use Stop notes to silence held notes.
Bend range
Sets the pitch wheel’s maximum travel in semitones from 0 to 24. Use 2 for a whole-tone bend or 12 for an octave. Sustain pedal uses CC64 and holds releases until you lift it.
Divisions · Period ratio
Divisions sets 1–99 equal steps per period. Period ratio sets the interval that repeats, from 1.001 to 16. For 19-EDO choose Use equal divisions, enter 19 and leave Period at 2. For 13 equal steps of a tritave, use 13 and 3.
Tuning files…
Choose Load SCL, KBM or TUN. SCL supplies a Scala scale. Select the SCL and its KBM together if the scale has a keyboard map. Numerical TUN data can supply per-note tuning. Show tuning information identifies the active tuning. Use equal divisions returns to the Divisions and Period controls.
Stop notes
Use the bottom-right button to silence held or stuck notes. If they start again immediately, check whether a playing DAW clip is still sending new notes.
‹ Oscillator and tooth shapeSpatial, orbit and mechanics ›
Operation manual   /   Control reference

Spatial, orbit and mechanics

Spatial controls work on the instrument’s stereo output. Try them on a non-root gear while a steady note is playing. Headphones make a small movement easier to follow.

Spatial pan · Pan (degrees)
Enable Spatial pan on the keyboard strip. The Pan knob sets an azimuth around the listener. It is a circular angle, so −180° and +180° meet. On a routed Pan knob, a sweep from 0° to 180° crosses from right to left.
Height / Z
−1 to +1. Move a non-root gear vertically to change its spatial colouring and level. Solo it briefly to judge the effect.
Orbit movement · direction
Enable a gear’s orbit to move it around the listener. Choose clockwise or counter-clockwise to reverse its path.
Orbit period · depth · phase
Period is the orbit time setting, 0.25–120 s. Depth (0–1) sets the radius contribution. Position can also contribute to radius. Phase (0–360°) sets the starting angle. Give two gears different phases for a wider moving layer.
Mechanical connection · CONNECT / DISCONNECT
In Mechanics choose a different gear and connect or disconnect the selected pair. A gear needs a path to the root to turn. Idle on its card is a clue to check the mechanical links. Keep a simple branching train if the network reports conflicting directions.
Phase offset
−360° to +360°. Offsets the gear cycle. Try shifting two otherwise similar gears and listen as the summed tone thins or fills out.
Acceleration
0–5,000 ms. Sets how quickly a gear follows a changing target frequency. Zero responds immediately. A slower follower can trail a fast bend.
Off-centre
0–100%. Introduces cyclical rate variation. Start with a few percent for gentle pitch movement. For an evolving wobble choose Off-centre as an envelope target.
Vinyl / eccentric playback
The checkbox is stored with the gear. In 0.3.6 the native playback calculation reads Off-centre directly. Use Off-centre to set the audible wobble.
Clockwork tick width
0.4–18 ms on the control. Adjust the strike shape of the Clockwork waveform. This setting is shared by Clockwork gears in the patch.
‹ Keyboard, tuning files and glissandoLoad a sample and edit its loop ›
Operation manual   /   Control reference

Load a sample and edit its loop

A recording can be a playable instrument, an audible texture in the train, or the signal that drives another gear’s FM.

  1. Select the gear, open Sample and choose Load sample. The picker accepts WAV, AIF/AIFF, FLAC and OGG. Loading selects Audio sample as the source and initially loops the whole recording. The native loader reads up to the first 180 seconds.
  2. Set Sample root note to the MIDI note of the recording. For a sample of A440, enter 69. Try it first on a 1:1 gear so the note is easy to check.
  3. Choose Edit waveform…. Drag either gold boundary to isolate a steady section. The readout shows seconds. Sample loop start and end in the inspector are fractions of the file, from its beginning to its end.
  4. Play several notes. A shorter loop can turn a field recording into a buzz. Use Volume ADSR to soften its entry and exit. Clear sample removes the loaded audio from the selected gear.
The sample loop repeats audio between two file positions. Loop sustain repeats a path drawn in an envelope. You can use them together or edit either one independently.
‹ Spatial, orbit and mechanicsPresets, Bloom and Master ›
Operation manual   /   Control reference

Presets, Bloom and Master

New instances open on SYNTH: PAD: Chordial. Reopening a saved session restores that instance’s project state.

Top preset selector · ‹ / ›
Choose a user patch or one of the 16 factory sounds. With the editor or visual focused, use the left and right arrow keys to step through the list live. It wraps at either end. When editing a text field, arrows belong to that field.
Load preset · Save preset
Load a .cog patch or choose a sound inside a .cogpack. Save preset writes an individual .cog. Save to the proposed User Presets folder to see the file alongside the factory list. Use a fresh name to keep a variation.
Master
Overall output, 0–1. Compare patches at similar levels. If the DAW meter clips when you add a gear or play a chord, turn Master down.
Bloom
From −5 to +5. With multiple audible gears, positive values open lower-ratio gears first and progressively lengthen higher gears’ attacks. Negative values reverse the order. Zero gives each gear its programmed attack. A looping volume envelope keeps its own cycle timing under the fade.
Bloom placement order
In Presets, enable this to stagger the gears in their placement order. Try it with three layers and Bloom around +1, then compare with pitch ordering.
Preset fade (s)
0–5 s. Controls the transition for sounding voices when switching presets. Try a long fade under a held chord. For fast comparisons use zero.
Network snapshot
The text panel under Presets summarises the current graph. Use it alongside card IDs when tracking a connection through a large patch.

Use the factory bank as listening material

Start with Happy New Gear when learning a single control. Open Chordial afterwards to hear how six gears interact. The figures below count the gears saved in each patch.

  • Happy New Gear · 1 gears
  • SYNTH: PAD: Wiggly Middle · 3 gears
  • SYNTH: LEADS: Bibble · 3 gears
  • Pee 'n' Ohh · 7 gears
  • SYNTH: LEAD: Electric Saw · 5 gears
  • Boeuff Jerky · 5 gears
  • Deal Strum · 5 gears
  • SYNTH: LEAD: COVID 19 · 7 gears
  • FX: Wonky Machine · 6 gears
  • FX: Beacons · 7 gears
  • Wobbly Bob · 6 gears
  • SYNTH: LEAD: Follow Me! · 3 gears
  • SYNTH: PAD: Chordial · 6 gears
  • SYNTH: PAD: Curly Slide · 6 gears
  • SYNTH: LEAD: Floating Gears · 6 gears
  • ORCHESTRAL: WOODWINDS: Oscar Floot · 4 gears
‹ Load a sample and edit its loopDetached visuals and FM scope ›
Operation manual   /   Control reference

Detached visuals and FM scope

Moiré opens in a separate window. You can keep the editor on your composing screen and move the visual to a second display.

Visual selector · Detach visual · Full screen
Choose Wave / Moiré, Neon, Steampunk or Visual off at the top. Detach visual reopens the display. Full screen enlarges it. Escape returns it to a window. Closing the visual leaves the instrument playable.
Steampunk · Neon
Both show the mechanical train. Steampunk uses brass spokes and races. Neon uses luminous outlines. Tooth ratios set relative speed and linked gears counter-rotate. Drag a gear to swing a branch around its parent. Branches can pass through one another. Spatial placement may also change when you move a gear.
Moiré controls
Move over the detached visual and open Moiré controls. Changing presets keeps your visual mode and Moiré settings. The Windows display uses Edge WebView2. The Linux display uses GTK 3 and WebKitGTK.
Scale · Modulation (%) · Modulation period (s)
Scale changes the pattern size (0.1–5). Modulation sets the amount of cyclic visual breathing, initially 10%. Period is the time for one cycle, 0.1–60 s. FM shake also influences the visible movement.
Brightness · Band width · Curvature
Brightness adjusts display intensity from 0 to 2. Band width (0–100) changes the stripe treatment. Curvature (−1 to +1) bends the pattern. Hold the same note while comparing these.
Rotation speed · FM shake
Rotation speed adjusts the visual motion rate. FM shake sets the amount of motion from FM, initially 10%. Reduce both for a calmer projection.
Penrose families
Switches to a quasiperiodic stripe arrangement. Try it on a held interval so you can watch the pattern form.
FM scope
Shows the actual mono sum of the stereo output, including every audible gear and voice. The view uses a rising-edge trigger. Scale changes the time window. A pure sine is expected for a lone sine oscillator. Add FM, another gear or a chord to see the combined wave.
Blend mode · Background · Media opacity
Try Screen or Add for luminous overlapping layers, or Multiply for a darker composite. Pick a background colour. Media opacity controls how strongly a loaded image or video appears.
Media underlay · Clear media
Choose a local image or video to layer beneath the pattern. Clear media removes it. Choose the media again when recreating the visual window. These settings affect the picture.
‹ Presets, Bloom and MasterMIDI learn, DAW automation and hardware ›
Operation manual   /   Working procedures

MIDI learn, DAW automation and hardware

MIDI carries gestures into TuneOut. Audio carries its sound out. Keeping those paths separate makes both recording and troubleshooting easier.

Record a performance and edit it later

  1. Select the TuneOut instrument track. Choose your keyboard as its MIDI input, enable monitoring or record-arm, and check that incoming notes light the editor keys.
  2. Record the part as MIDI. Edit its notes, velocity, sustain pedal or pitch bend in the DAW. A MIDI clip also makes a repeatable phrase for comparing presets.
  3. For automation lanes, the exposed globals are Fundamental, Master Volume, Just Intonation Chords, Polyphonic, Spatial Pan, Pitch Bend Range, Bloom, Tuning divisions, Tuning period ratio and Preset crossfade. Use learned CC data for the four knobs on individual gears.
  4. When the sound is ready, render, freeze or bounce the instrument using the DAW. Include enough time after the last note for Volume Release and any effects on the track.

Put a hardware knob on one gear

  1. Connect the controller by USB MIDI or an interface MIDI input. Pick an unused knob that sends a continuous controller, for example CC74 on channel 1. Route that input to the instrument track.
  2. Right-click the receiving gear’s FM knob, choose MIDI Learn, then move only that hardware knob. Look for the CC number above the card knob and the channel in its context menu.
  3. Hold a note and record a slow turn into the MIDI part. If you want a smaller sweep, set the Min / Max endpoints, apply the range, then choose Remove modulation to use the learned CC over those endpoints.
  4. To change controllers, use MIDI Learn again. If the sustain pedal was learned by accident, use Clear MIDI assignment. CC64 also operates sustain, so a different CC is easier to use for tone control.

Send the sound through an external pedal or processor

Use the DAW or interface to send the instrument’s audio to a spare physical output. Connect that output to the processor, then return the processor’s output to an interface input. Match the hardware’s input level, start with a low send, and monitor the return on a separate audio track. Keep that return out of the hardware send to avoid a feedback loop. Record the return when you like the take.

For an external synth playing alongside TuneOut, route a copy of the MIDI part from the DAW to the external synth’s port and record its audio separately. The VST3 receives host MIDI and produces audio. The DAW handles external MIDI destinations, audio devices, transport and recording.

‹ Detached visuals and FM scopeTroubleshooting ›
Operation manual   /   Working procedures

Troubleshooting

Change one thing at a time. Happy New Gear and a single held note make a useful reference.

The DAW cannot find TuneOut
Extract the entire ZIP and run the installer with the DAW closed. The complete TuneOut.vst3 folder belongs under C:\Program Files\Common Files\VST3. In Nuendo 14 check Studio → VST Plug-in Manager → VST Instruments, the active collection and the Blocklist. The included Check TuneOut.cmd writes a scan report.
I can click notes but my controller is silent
The instrument is making audio. Check the DAW track’s MIDI input, monitoring and record arm. If the keys light but you hear silence, check Master, the output bus, Solo/Mute, gear connections and Volume ADSR.
FM barely changes the note
Check the receiver’s IN label, FM enabled and index. Use Direct first. Set the source to an oscillator and connect it mechanically to the root. Turn down the sender’s audible Volume to hear the receiver clearly.
The Aux graph moves but I hear no sweep
Check the AUX label on the intended knob, Aux Enabled, Depth, and the minimum and maximum. For FM, the receiver needs a source. For Pan, enable Spatial pan. A short Volume Release can hide a long Aux Release.
The loop sounds late or motionless
Check Attack and Decay on the envelope you routed, then expand it. A sustain loop needs different point levels to reveal its motion. A 5 s sustain window with the first change near its end may sound almost still. Test a 0.35 s window with a prominent early point.
The note lingers or slides
Lift the sustain pedal, check Volume Release and Hold mono notes, then use Stop notes. If successive notes slide, check Gliss and gear Acceleration.
A tuning sounds familiar when I expected new intervals
Confirm the scale name on the keyboard strip. For equal divisions, enter both Divisions and Period. Disable JI for an exact comparison and play the same MIDI notes again.
The visual is missing or the scope is flat
Choose Wave / Moiré and Detach visual. Check Brightness and your platform’s web-view runtime if the display reports it is needed. A flat scope means there is little or no summed output. Check a sustained Happy New Gear note before diagnosing a complex patch.
‹ MIDI learn, DAW automation and hardwareBasic curves and powers ›
Operation manual   /   FM equation reference

Basic curves and powers

Each example uses a 440 Hz carrier, a 220 Hz sender and index 1. The two frequencies give the result for negative and positive half-scale sender samples. Select a name to inspect its entire curve.

Direct

Passes the source value straight through. A sine modulator makes the pitch swing smoothly above and below the carrier at the modulator rate.

At −0.50 330.00 Hz   ·   At +0.50 550.00 Hz

power

Raises the source magnitude to 0.1 + half the index, then restores its sign. Exponents below one magnify small bends. Above one, most of the deviation gathers near the source peaks.

At −0.50 294.85 Hz   ·   At +0.50 585.15 Hz

sqrt

Takes the square root of the source magnitude and restores its sign. Half-scale input already delivers about 71% of a full bend at index 1.

At −0.50 284.44 Hz   ·   At +0.50 595.56 Hz

cbrt

Takes the cube root. A positive or negative eighth-scale input becomes a half-scale bend, so even small movements pull the carrier strongly.

At −0.50 265.39 Hz   ·   At +0.50 614.61 Hz

nroot

Takes a signed root whose order is one plus the whole-number part of the index. Crossing an integer changes the curve as well as the depth.

At −0.50 284.44 Hz   ·   At +0.50 595.56 Hz

square

Squares the magnitude and preserves direction. A half-scale input produces a quarter-scale bend at index 1. The pitch stays nearer home around source zero crossings.

At −0.50 385.00 Hz   ·   At +0.50 495.00 Hz

cube

Cubes the input. Half-scale becomes one eighth, concentrating the fastest pitch excursions at the peaks of the source.

At −0.50 412.50 Hz   ·   At +0.50 467.50 Hz

quartic

Raises magnitude to the fourth power with the original sign. At half scale the deviation is only one sixteenth of full depth.

At −0.50 426.25 Hz   ·   At +0.50 453.75 Hz

quintic

Raises magnitude to the fifth power. Much of a sine cycle passes close to the carrier frequency before each peak gives a strong bend.

At −0.50 433.12 Hz   ·   At +0.50 446.88 Hz

inverse

Divides the input by its square plus 0.04. Small inputs climb rapidly, medium inputs hit the bend limit, and the response eases towards the outer edge.

At −0.50 220.00 Hz   ·   At +0.50 660.00 Hz

log

Uses a signed logarithm normalized at full scale. Small inputs gain leverage, with a more gradual rise towards maximum deviation.

At −0.50 311.31 Hz   ·   At +0.50 568.69 Hz

log10

Uses the same normalized logarithmic curve in base ten. The change of base cancels in the normalization, giving the same pitch trajectory as log.

At −0.50 311.31 Hz   ·   At +0.50 568.69 Hz

log2

Uses the normalized logarithm in base two. Its frequency response matches log and log10 to rounding precision.

At −0.50 311.31 Hz   ·   At +0.50 568.69 Hz

exp

Uses a normalized exponential. The bend starts gently, then steepens near either peak as the index rises.

At −0.50 356.94 Hz   ·   At +0.50 523.06 Hz

exp2

Uses powers of two. On a sweep from zero to full input, more of the deviation arrives late than with Direct.

At −0.50 348.87 Hz   ·   At +0.50 531.13 Hz

exp10

Uses powers of ten. Compared at the same index, it concentrates bends near full input more strongly than exp2.

At −0.50 387.14 Hz   ·   At +0.50 492.86 Hz
‹ TroubleshootingTrigonometric functions ›
Operation manual   /   FM equation reference

Trigonometric functions

Each example uses a 440 Hz carrier, a 220 Hz sender and index 1. The two frequencies give the result for negative and positive half-scale sender samples. Select a name to inspect its entire curve.

sin

Maps input through sin(π × input × index). At index 1, positive half-scale gives the maximum upward bend and positive full-scale brings pitch home.

At −0.50 220.00 Hz   ·   At +0.50 660.00 Hz

cos

Multiplies cosine by the source sign. Just above zero the bend can be large and positive, then turn down and reverse within the same positive half-cycle.

At −0.50 440.00 Hz   ·   At +0.50 440.00 Hz

tan

Uses a tangent softened by tanh. Bends rapidly approach their limits, and crossing a tangent pole reverses direction sharply.

At −0.50 272.45 Hz   ·   At +0.50 607.55 Hz

csc

Uses an inverse absolute sine with a small denominator offset. Source levels near sine zeros give the largest bends, with the source sign setting the direction.

At −0.50 236.30 Hz   ·   At +0.50 643.70 Hz

sec

Uses an inverse absolute cosine. The greatest bends occur near cosine zeros, shifting the accents relative to csc.

At −0.50 220.00 Hz   ·   At +0.50 660.00 Hz

cot

Divides cosine by a softened absolute sine and restores the source sign. Peaks are limited and the bend reverses where cosine changes sign.

At −0.50 440.00 Hz   ·   At +0.50 440.00 Hz

asin

Uses a normalized arcsine. The pitch moves gently near the middle of the input range and steeply near its edges.

At −0.50 366.67 Hz   ·   At +0.50 513.33 Hz

acos

Uses a signed, rescaled arccosine of magnitude. Its implemented curve equals the normalized arcsine, so compare it with asin for a matching bend.

At −0.50 366.67 Hz   ·   At +0.50 513.33 Hz

atan

Uses arctangent. The bend grows smoothly and flattens as input magnitude or index rises.

At −0.50 375.06 Hz   ·   At +0.50 504.94 Hz

atan2

Measures the angle of the input against 0.35 plus its magnitude. This produces a modest, smoothly bounded pitch excursion.

At −0.50 365.53 Hz   ·   At +0.50 514.47 Hz
‹ Basic curves and powersHyperbolic functions ›
Operation manual   /   FM equation reference

Hyperbolic functions

Each example uses a 440 Hz carrier, a 220 Hz sender and index 1. The two frequencies give the result for negative and positive half-scale sender samples. Select a name to inspect its entire curve.

sinh

Uses signed normalized hyperbolic sine. It emphasizes the source peaks, with the inner argument capped at five.

At −0.50 342.45 Hz   ·   At +0.50 537.55 Hz

cosh

Uses hyperbolic cosine minus one, then restores the sign. It begins flat near zero, making the larger source values do most of the bending.

At −0.50 388.30 Hz   ·   At +0.50 491.70 Hz

tanh

Uses hyperbolic tangent. Increasing index gives broad, nearly level stretches at the upper and lower bend limits.

At −0.50 338.33 Hz   ·   At +0.50 541.67 Hz

csch

Uses inverse hyperbolic sine magnitude with an offset in the denominator. Just off zero the bend is strong, falling away as source magnitude rises.

At −0.50 220.00 Hz   ·   At +0.50 660.00 Hz

sech

Uses the reciprocal of hyperbolic cosine, with source sign. The bend is largest just either side of zero and shrinks towards the peaks.

At −0.50 244.90 Hz   ·   At +0.50 635.10 Hz

coth

Uses the reciprocal of a bounded tanh, then applies the source sign. Its magnitude reaches the output clamp at full wet mix, giving two main pitch levels.

At −0.50 220.00 Hz   ·   At +0.50 660.00 Hz

asinh

Uses normalized inverse hyperbolic sine. Low inputs move the pitch readily, with progressively softer growth towards full excursion.

At −0.50 319.88 Hz   ·   At +0.50 560.12 Hz

acosh

Uses normalized acosh of one plus the scaled magnitude. The pitch changes quickly as the source leaves zero, then more slowly near its peaks.

At −0.50 279.23 Hz   ·   At +0.50 600.77 Hz

atanh

Uses a bounded inverse tanh. Large inputs have a steeper response, while an input ceiling keeps the bend finite.

At −0.50 337.71 Hz   ·   At +0.50 542.29 Hz
‹ Trigonometric functionsComplex transforms ›
Operation manual   /   FM equation reference

Complex transforms

Each example uses a 440 Hz carrier, a 220 Hz sender and index 1. The two frequencies give the result for negative and positive half-scale sender samples. Select a name to inspect its entire curve.

complex magnitude

Uses a signed square root. Its frequency curve is the same as sqrt.

At −0.50 284.44 Hz   ·   At +0.50 595.56 Hz

complex phase

Converts the source to the angle atan2(input, 1). At full-scale input the transformed magnitude is one half, giving a restrained pitch swing.

At −0.50 375.06 Hz   ·   At +0.50 504.94 Hz

conjugate

Reverses the source sign. Wherever Direct would bend upward this bends downward by the same amount.

At −0.50 550.00 Hz   ·   At +0.50 330.00 Hz

reciprocal

Divides input by its square plus 0.05. Bends climb rapidly around zero and fold back towards the ends, much like inverse with a slightly softer denominator.

At −0.50 220.00 Hz   ·   At +0.50 660.00 Hz

abs square

Uses magnitude squared with the original sign. Its curve matches square and Einstein mass energy.

At −0.50 385.00 Hz   ·   At +0.50 495.00 Hz
‹ Hyperbolic functionsPhysics-inspired functions ›
Operation manual   /   FM equation reference

Physics-inspired functions

Each example uses a 440 Hz carrier, a 220 Hz sender and index 1. The two frequencies give the result for negative and positive half-scale sender samples. Select a name to inspect its entire curve.

schrodinger

Applies a signed power with a Gaussian taper. The power cycles through five orders as the index crosses integers, changing which parts of the source cycle bend the pitch most.

At −0.50 389.61 Hz   ·   At +0.50 490.39 Hz

heisenberg

Divides input by one plus twice its scaled magnitude. The curve compresses large values, limiting the outward bend.

At −0.50 385.00 Hz   ·   At +0.50 495.00 Hz

einstein mass energy

Squares the magnitude and restores the sign. Quarter, half and full positive input produce 1/16, 1/4 and full upward deviation at index 1. The negative half bends down symmetrically.

At −0.50 385.00 Hz   ·   At +0.50 495.00 Hz

planck radiation

Divides a cubic magnitude by an exponential denominator. Small inputs cause little deviation. At larger index the exponential can suppress the outer bends too.

At −0.50 396.19 Hz   ·   At +0.50 483.81 Hz

maxwell boltzmann

Weights the squared source magnitude by a falling exponential and restores direction. At index 1 and above its shape is fixed while the outer FM depth keeps increasing.

At −0.50 360.04 Hz   ·   At +0.50 519.96 Hz

wave equation

Uses a sine whose multiplier advances in whole steps with index and repeats after eight. Each extra fold lets the carrier reverse its bend more often during one source cycle.

At −0.50 440.00 Hz   ·   At +0.50 440.00 Hz

heat equation

Multiplies input by a decaying exponential. Increasing index damps the outer excursions and can place the strongest bend partway through the source swing.

At −0.50 352.16 Hz   ·   At +0.50 527.84 Hz

lorentz factor

Uses a bounded speed-like value in a relativistic-factor curve. The middle remains gentle while high inputs pull away more rapidly.

At −0.50 439.23 Hz   ·   At +0.50 440.77 Hz

schwarzschild

Divides input by a denominator that shrinks towards the peaks. Strong input values exaggerate the pitch displacement until the output clamps.

At −0.50 325.42 Hz   ·   At +0.50 554.58 Hz

compton scattering

Divides input by an angle-dependent factor. At a given index the extremes are reduced relative to Direct.

At −0.50 345.17 Hz   ·   At +0.50 534.83 Hz
‹ Complex transformsSpecial functions ›
Operation manual   /   FM equation reference

Special functions

Each example uses a 440 Hz carrier, a 220 Hz sender and index 1. The two frequencies give the result for negative and positive half-scale sender samples. Select a name to inspect its entire curve.

gamma

Uses a bounded approximation based on log-gamma, then restores the sign. It can jump as the input crosses zero and its outer bends change with index.

At −0.50 293.93 Hz   ·   At +0.50 586.07 Hz

factorial

Raises one plus the magnitude to a power, normalizes at full scale and restores sign. The pitch already jumps just off zero before moving further near the peak.

At −0.50 275.00 Hz   ·   At +0.50 605.00 Hz

zeta

Uses sign divided by one plus scaled magnitude. Small nonzero inputs create a strong bend and larger inputs bring the pitch closer to centre.

At −0.50 293.33 Hz   ·   At +0.50 586.67 Hz

eta

Balances a rising exponential term against a growing denominator. The bend rises from zero and can recede at the outer end.

At −0.50 370.75 Hz   ·   At +0.50 509.25 Hz

bessel j0

Uses a signed sine lobe divided by its argument plus an offset. As magnitude increases, deviation alternates direction with progressively smaller lobes.

At −0.50 304.26 Hz   ·   At +0.50 575.74 Hz

bessel y0

Uses a cosine lobe over a softened denominator. Strong near-zero excursions give way to smaller alternating bends.

At −0.50 440.00 Hz   ·   At +0.50 440.00 Hz

bessel i0

Applies hyperbolic cosine minus one with bounded arguments. It suppresses low-level bends and brings in the strongest variation near source peaks.

At −0.50 421.80 Hz   ·   At +0.50 458.20 Hz

bessel k0

Combines a falling exponential with an inverse square root. Very small nonzero inputs make large bends, which diminish quickly as the magnitude grows.

At −0.50 260.07 Hz   ·   At +0.50 619.93 Hz

airy ai

Uses sine with a phase proportional to magnitude raised to 1.5 and a gentle taper. Bends change direction more closely together towards stronger inputs.

At −0.50 374.25 Hz   ·   At +0.50 505.75 Hz

airy bi

Uses the cosine partner of airy ai. It starts near a strong bend just off zero and progressively folds towards the outer input levels.

At −0.50 262.43 Hz   ·   At +0.50 617.57 Hz

erf

Uses a signed approximation to the error function. The frequency shift grows smoothly from zero towards a rounded plateau.

At −0.50 325.49 Hz   ·   At +0.50 554.51 Hz

erfc

Uses the complementary error function with source sign. Excursions are strongest just off zero and fade as the source grows.

At −0.50 334.51 Hz   ·   At +0.50 545.49 Hz
‹ Physics-inspired functionsMaps and spirals ›
Operation manual   /   FM equation reference

Maps and spirals

Each example uses a 440 Hz carrier, a 220 Hz sender and index 1. The two frequencies give the result for negative and positive half-scale sender samples. Select a name to inspect its entire curve.

mobius

Uses a signed fractional-linear curve with an offset. The frequency changes by a small step on crossing zero, then follows a compressed rise.

At −0.50 334.00 Hz   ·   At +0.50 546.00 Hz

joukowsky

Blends a linear magnitude with a reciprocal term. Pitch can bend strongly just off zero, ease inward and then grow again.

At −0.50 369.83 Hz   ·   At +0.50 510.17 Hz

schwarz christoffel

Multiplies a power-shaped magnitude by sine. The outer input values carry the strongest folds and may bend the carrier in opposite directions.

At −0.50 255.00 Hz   ·   At +0.50 625.00 Hz

cayley

Divides input by its magnitude plus an index-dependent offset. This rounds the bend towards a ceiling.

At −0.50 268.12 Hz   ·   At +0.50 611.88 Hz

spiral

Multiplies input by a cosine of its magnitude. Sign changes in that cosine reverse the direction of the bend within each source half-cycle.

At −0.50 550.00 Hz   ·   At +0.50 330.00 Hz

fibonacci spiral

Uses the fractional part of a golden-ratio power to scale a sine. Each wrap of that fraction abruptly changes the bend size.

At −0.50 380.16 Hz   ·   At +0.50 499.84 Hz

archimedean spiral

Multiplies a sine of magnitude by the magnitude itself and restores sign. The alternating bends widen near the source peaks.

At −0.50 440.00 Hz   ·   At +0.50 440.00 Hz

fermat spiral

Weights a sine by the square root of magnitude. It brings out inner folds more strongly than a linear magnitude weighting.

At −0.50 284.44 Hz   ·   At +0.50 595.56 Hz

hyperbolic spiral

Uses sign divided by one plus three times scaled magnitude. Its largest excursions sit just off the zero crossing and decay rapidly.

At −0.50 352.00 Hz   ·   At +0.50 528.00 Hz

ulam spiral

Multiplies a wrapping fractional ramp by a sine. Pitch follows each ramp until the fraction resets at the next integer.

At −0.50 330.00 Hz   ·   At +0.50 550.00 Hz
‹ Special functionsFractals and dynamical maps ›
Operation manual   /   FM equation reference

Fractals and dynamical maps

Each example uses a 440 Hz carrier, a 220 Hz sender and index 1. The two frequencies give the result for negative and positive half-scale sender samples. Select a name to inspect its entire curve.

mandelbrot

Runs up to six quadratic iterations from zero. The source and index choose a point; its escape count selects a pitch-bend level. Nearby source amplitudes can land on the same step or jump apart.

At −0.50 220.00 Hz   ·   At +0.50 660.00 Hz

julia

Uses the source as the starting real coordinate, and an index-dependent complex constant. Up to six escape checks select a stepped bend, with thresholds in different places from Mandelbrot.

At −0.50 220.00 Hz   ·   At +0.50 660.00 Hz

burning ship

Takes absolute values of the real and imaginary components before the quadratic update. This folds the escape path and relocates the pitch steps.

At −0.50 220.00 Hz   ·   At +0.50 660.00 Hz

tricorn

Reverses the sign of the imaginary part of the quadratic update. Up to six checks give a different staircase of carrier deviations.

At −0.50 220.00 Hz   ·   At +0.50 660.00 Hz

multibrot

Raises the complex value to a power of two, three or four, selected by index. A five-iteration escape count sets the pitch step.

At −0.50 220.00 Hz   ·   At +0.50 660.00 Hz

newton raphson

Takes one softened Newton update towards a cube root of one, then applies tanh. Even zero source input can produce an upward shift at a full wet mix.

At −0.50 592.66 Hz   ·   At +0.50 641.19 Hz

nova

Adds an index-scaled input term to a softened Newton update. This changes the tilt and the balance of upward and downward bends.

At −0.50 581.49 Hz   ·   At +0.50 642.41 Hz

phoenix

Makes four quadratic updates, each using the preceding value as well. The final value is softened and signed. The four steps restart for every source sample.

At −0.50 515.71 Hz   ·   At +0.50 374.91 Hz

magnet

Passes a ratio of two quadratic expressions through tanh. The numerator crosses zero at half-scale magnitude, reversing the bend there.

At −0.50 440.00 Hz   ·   At +0.50 440.00 Hz

lambda

Runs four logistic updates from the rescaled input. The final position chooses the shift, so a smooth source sweeps through several folds.

At −0.50 423.85 Hz   ·   At +0.50 456.15 Hz

spider

Runs four complex quadratic updates while letting the real constant follow the evolving value. The final real coordinate supplies the bend.

At −0.50 524.15 Hz   ·   At +0.50 419.65 Hz

henon map

Runs four coupled Hénon-style updates and reads the softened final coordinate. Neighbouring input levels can then give bends of different size or sign.

At −0.50 479.13 Hz   ·   At +0.50 450.63 Hz

lorenz attractor

Uses a single Lorenz-inspired slope estimate and tanh. This version gives a smooth, slightly offset curve for each input sample.

At −0.50 391.24 Hz   ·   At +0.50 491.83 Hz

logistic map

Runs five logistic updates with an index-dependent multiplier. Moving the index shifts the fine folds in the carrier’s deviation.

At −0.50 434.37 Hz   ·   At +0.50 445.63 Hz

tent map

Folds a triangle-shaped map four times. The result gives sharp linear ramps and direction changes across the input range.

Waves and pulses

Each example uses a 440 Hz carrier, a 220 Hz sender and index 1. The two frequencies give the result for negative and positive half-scale sender samples. Select a name to inspect its entire curve.

wave

Uses sin(2π × input × index). The bend crosses centre repeatedly as the source sweeps through its range.

At −0.50 440.00 Hz   ·   At +0.50 440.00 Hz

ripple

Uses a damped sine of source magnitude. Its alternating pitch excursions get smaller farther from the middle.

At −0.50 440.00 Hz   ·   At +0.50 440.00 Hz

standing wave

Uses a sine with an integer multiplier. Crossing a whole-number index adds another fold across the source range.

At −0.50 440.00 Hz   ·   At +0.50 440.00 Hz

beat frequency

Multiplies sine by a second cosine. The bends grow and shrink across the input range, creating a beat-like pattern in deviation.

At −0.50 440.00 Hz   ·   At +0.50 440.00 Hz

doppler effect

Uses a sine divided by a magnitude-dependent factor. The outer bends soften while the sine can still reverse direction.

At −0.50 235.35 Hz   ·   At +0.50 644.65 Hz

gaussian wave

Weights the source with a Gaussian. Small and intermediate values bend readily while a large index draws the extremes back towards centre.

At −0.50 364.40 Hz   ·   At +0.50 515.60 Hz

sinc function

Uses signed sinc of scaled magnitude. The pitch jumps near zero, then follows progressively smaller lobes, with reversals as the sine changes sign.

At −0.50 299.94 Hz   ·   At +0.50 580.06 Hz

chirp

Uses sine of the squared magnitude. The resulting bends are spaced farther apart near zero and closer together towards the peaks.

At −0.50 440.00 Hz   ·   At +0.50 440.00 Hz

morlet wavelet

Combines a fast sine with a Gaussian taper. A cluster of alternating bends around the centre fades towards the edges.

At −0.50 319.37 Hz   ·   At +0.50 560.63 Hz

mexican hat

Uses a Gaussian weighted by one minus squared magnitude. The deviation changes sign when scaled magnitude crosses one.

At −0.50 294.39 Hz   ·   At +0.50 585.61 Hz

dirac delta

Uses a narrow Gaussian with the source sign. Most deviation is concentrated near zero crossings, giving short bursts of pitch movement.

At −0.50 439.45 Hz   ·   At +0.50 440.55 Hz

heaviside step

Returns the sign of the source. At index 1, negative and positive inputs select two frequency levels; exact zero returns the carrier to its base rate.

At −0.50 220.00 Hz   ·   At +0.50 660.00 Hz

sawtooth

Wraps the scaled input into a repeating ramp. Each wrap jumps directly from one edge of the deviation range to the other.

At −0.50 220.00 Hz   ·   At +0.50 220.00 Hz

square wave

Uses the sign of a sine to choose full upward or downward deviation. It can switch several times within a single half-cycle of the modulator.

At −0.50 220.00 Hz   ·   At +0.50 660.00 Hz

triangle wave

Folds a sine into a triangle. The frequency follows linear ramps between its upper and lower deviations.

At −0.50 440.00 Hz   ·   At +0.50 440.00 Hz

pulse train

Opens a narrow gate near multiples of the scaled input. Inside the gate the source sign selects full bend; between gates the pitch returns to base.

Quantum-inspired functions

Each example uses a 440 Hz carrier, a 220 Hz sender and index 1. The two frequencies give the result for negative and positive half-scale sender samples. Select a name to inspect its entire curve.

quantum harmonic

Multiplies a Gaussian by one minus twice the squared scaled input. A central lobe bends one way and the outer lobes reverse.

At −0.50 342.93 Hz   ·   At +0.50 537.07 Hz

hydrogen orbital

Weights the signed square by a decaying exponential. Small inputs cause little movement, with the outer range increasingly damped at high index.

At −0.50 399.25 Hz   ·   At +0.50 480.75 Hz

tunneling effect

Multiplies input by a falling exponential. As the index rises the strongest excursions concentrate closer to zero.

At −0.50 366.26 Hz   ·   At +0.50 513.74 Hz

klein gordon

Uses a sine of the square root of squared input plus squared index, restoring source sign. The index can reposition a whole half-cycle above or below the centre frequency.

At −0.50 223.77 Hz   ·   At +0.50 656.23 Hz

dirac equation

Divides input by a square-root factor. This compresses the strongest excursions while retaining bend direction.

At −0.50 336.29 Hz   ·   At +0.50 543.71 Hz

feynman diagram

Uses a softened reciprocal with an index-dependent denominator. Small changes around zero can create pronounced shifts, especially at lower index.
